Time Management In Performance; Series 1 Knowing When to Hold, Flow, Adapt and Let Go. Series 1 — Time Is a Framework, Not a Prison Every professional performer needs to understand the difference between managing time and being controlled by time. A performer must respect time without becoming a prisoner of it. A set list, programme, rehearsal plan or allocated performance slot provides direction. But a live performance is not always predictable. The audience may respond differently, a musical moment may become unusually powerful, or a song may require more space than anticipated. The goal is not simply to “finish everything on the list.” The goal is to communicate. As a music coach, I have learned that a performance cannot always be reduced to a stopwatch. A set list may say six songs in 40 minutes, but the purpose of those 40 minutes is not merely to prove that six songs can be completed. The purpose is communication. For example, a choir may prepare four songs for a 30-minute presentation. During the second song, the audience responds strongly to a particular musical phrase. The director may allow the phrase to breathe, repeat a section or extend a transition—without abandoning the arrangement. That is professional flexibility. However, flexibility requires preparation. When musicians know their music, structure and cues, they can respond naturally without creating confusion. The clock still matters. The programme still matters. The organiser’s instructions still matter. But the clock should help shape the performance, not destroy its musicality. Good time management therefore means knowing the plan well enough to adapt intelligently. “Time should guide a performance, not imprison the creativity that makes the performance meaningful.” — Victor Adenola #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #creativity #musicDirector #musicians #musicperformance #musicproduction #performance #performancetips #practicing #rehearsal #singers #singersgospelSingers #stageconfidence

Time Management In Performance; Series 1 Knowing When to Hold, Flow, Adapt and Let Go. Series 1 — Time Is a Framework, Not a Prison Every professional performer needs to understand the difference between managing time and being controlled by time. A performer must respect time without becoming a prisoner of it. A set list, programme, rehearsal plan or allocated performance slot provides direction. But a live performance is not always predictable. The audience may respond differently, a musical moment may become unusually powerful, or a song may require more space than anticipated. The goal is not simply to “finish everything on the list.” The goal is to communicate. As a music coach, I have learned that a performance cannot always be reduced to a stopwatch. A set list may say six songs in 40 minutes, but the purpose of those 40 minutes is not merely to prove that six songs can be completed. The purpose is communication. For example, a choir may prepare four songs for a 30-minute presentation. During the second song, the audience responds strongly to a particular musical phrase. The director may allow the phrase to breathe, repeat a section or extend a transition—without abandoning the arrangement. That is professional flexibility. However, flexibility requires preparation. When musicians know their music, structure and cues, they can respond naturally without creating confusion. The clock still matters. The programme still matters. The organiser’s instructions still matter. But the clock should help shape the performance, not destroy its musicality. Good time management therefore means knowing the plan well enough to adapt intelligently. “Time should guide a performance, not imprison the creativity that makes the performance meaningful.” — Victor Adenola #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #creativity #musicDirector #musicians #musicperformance #musicproduction #performance #performancetips #practicing #rehearsal #singers #singersgospelSingers #stageconfidence
